approachQuestion.prompt:
Times for checkpoint visits

Each of n checkpoint requests gives a closed interval [start,end] during which one visit would satisfy it. One visit at time t satisfies every request containing t. Return the minimum number of visit times needed to satisfy all requests. The requests are unsorted and immutable; return only the count.

Input: requests = [[1,4],[3,7],[6,9],[8,10]]
Output: 2
Visits at 4 and 9 suffice.

Input: requests = [[2,2],[2,5],[5,5]]
Output: 2

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; integer endpoints satisfy 0 ≤ start ≤ end ≤ 1000000000. Visits may occur at any real time, including endpoints. Use comparison-based ordering and choose the best worst-case time.

options.text: Sort copied requests by end. When the current request is not covered by the last visit, place a new visit exactly at its end. Count visits.
options.feedback: The earliest-ending uncovered request needs a visit no later than its end. Moving that visit to its end still covers that request and cannot hurt any remaining request it previously covered.

options.text: Merge overlapping requests into connected union components and use one visit for each component.
options.feedback: A chain of overlaps need not share one point. For [[1,3],[2,5],[4,6]], the union is connected but no single time satisfies the first and last requests; 2 visits are needed.

options.text: Sort by start and place a visit at the start of each request not already covered.
options.feedback: For [[1,4],[2,5]], visiting at 1 then 2 uses 2 visits although one visit at 4 satisfies both.

options.text: Enumerate all subsets of the integer times from the smallest start through the largest end and choose the smallest satisfying subset.
options.feedback: Integer endpoints ensure an integer optimum exists, so this can find a correct answer. But enumerating subsets of a potentially billion-point domain is brute force far beyond what ordered endpoints require.

feedback.reason: Distinguish a common point from a connected union; satisfy intervals at a safe latest visit time.
details: Copy requests, sort by end using iterative bottom-up merge sort and a reusable buffer, then scan once with only the last visit time, a flag for no visits yet, and the count.

A visit at the earliest-finishing unmet request's end serves it while preserving every overlap with later-ending requests. Skip requests already containing the last visit. Endpoint inclusion makes choosing the end legal here.

“Sort copied requests by end. When the current request is not covered by the last visit, place a new visit exactly at its end. Count visits.”: The earliest-ending uncovered request needs a visit no later than its end. Moving that visit to its end still covers that request and cannot hurt any remaining request it previously covered.

“Merge overlapping requests into connected union components and use one visit for each component.”: A chain of overlaps need not share one point. For [[1,3],[2,5],[4,6]], the union is connected but no single time satisfies the first and last requests; 2 visits are needed.
“Sort by start and place a visit at the start of each request not already covered.”: For [[1,4],[2,5]], visiting at 1 then 2 uses 2 visits although one visit at 4 satisfies both.

“Enumerate all subsets of the integer times from the smallest start through the largest end and choose the smallest satisfying subset.”: Integer endpoints ensure an integer optimum exists, so this can find a correct answer. But enumerating subsets of a potentially billion-point domain is brute force far beyond what ordered endpoints require.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For visit-at-earliest-end, n is the request count. Include the copy and sort buffer in auxiliary space. Choose the tightest standard worst-case pair.
constraints: Analyze only the named method. Count all temporary arrays and the call stack; exclude the supplied input and returned output. Numeric comparisons, assignments and arithmetic take constant time, with no overflow.
No hashing or amortized data structure is used. All loops and binary searches are iterative; there is no recursive stack.

options.text: Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(1)
Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)

feedback.reason: Sorting requests dominates constant-state greedy selection.
details: The sort dominates the linear scan. Both copied requests and reusable merge buffer are linear; all scan state is constant and iterative. The number of coordinate values between endpoints does not enter the complexity.
Comparison ordering; iterative merge sort of an immutable-input copy.
“Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(1)”: The copied requests and merge buffer are auxiliary storage; the constant scan state is only part of memory use.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(n)”: The algorithm never compares every pair of requests. One comparison sort and one scan are sufficient.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: Ordering the unsorted requests by end via comparison merge sort is not linear in the worst case.
